mappings.note: Assertion-reason: air is matter because it occupies space and has mass. The two measurable quantities that define matter, LO-59.

Which statements hold -- one object can use several materials, one material can make many objects, and materials differ in properties. Identifying materials and what they make, LO-53. The stem retains only the last of the three numbered statements.

Which property matters most for a frying pan -- heat resistance and conduction. Matching a property to a required use, LO-62. Heat conduction is NEP content this frame's classification LOs do not name.
Slips as protective and decorative coats on Harappan pottery. A history-of-technology item; no LO covers ancient craft technique, so the goal about making things from available materials.
Why grouping by material is useful -- same material, similar properties and uses. The rationale for classification, LO-55.
Rough or smooth to the touch is texture. LO-53 names texture among its observable features.
A substance used to create an object is a material. The basic identification, LO-53.
Earliest Indian pottery was made of clay. Naming a material, LO-53.
Baked clay is terra-cotta. Naming a material, LO-53.
Arranging objects into groups by common properties is classification. LO-55's own definition.
What property a tumbler material needs -- it must hold water. Matching property to purpose, LO-62.
Whether one object can be made from several materials. Identification of materials within an object, LO-53.
Shiny surfaces mean a lustrous appearance. Naming an observable feature, LO-53.
Give an example of a metal. Identifying a material by name, LO-53.
Materials without shine are non-lustrous. Naming a property class, LO-55.
Easily compressed or scratched means soft. Naming a property class, LO-55.
Materials you can see through clearly are transparent. One of LO-55's three optical classes.
Give an opaque example. Placing a material in an LO-55 class.
Materials you see through unclearly are translucent. An LO-55 optical class.
Sugar dissolves when stirred in water. Placing sugar in the soluble class, LO-55.
Materials that do not mix with water are insoluble. An LO-55 class.
Dissolved oxygen matters for aquatic survival. A property tied to a consequence for living things, LO-57, consistent with the MCQ version of this item.
How heavy or light an object is describes its mass. Naming the physical quantity, LO-59.
The space water takes in a tumbler is its volume. Naming the physical quantity, LO-59.
Mass and volume as the two properties defining matter. The measurable quantities, LO-59.
Anything with mass occupying space is matter. Defined through its two measurable quantities, LO-59.
Material choice follows from properties and purpose. LO-62's principle.
Why cloth cannot store water -- water seeps through. The cause is the marked answer here, LO-57.
What lustre is, plus two lustrous metals. Identification by an observable feature, LO-53.
Why metals lose lustre -- air and moisture act on the surface. A phenomenon related to its cause, LO-57.
Differentiate hard from soft by compressibility. The verb and the property basis are LO-54's own.
Rubber is harder than sponge but softer than iron. Hardness as a RELATIVE comparison between materials, which is differentiation, LO-54, not a fixed class.
Define transparent materials with two examples. An LO-55 optical class.
Define opaque materials with two examples. An LO-55 optical class.
Define translucent materials with two examples. An LO-55 optical class.
What soluble means, with an example. LO-55's own solubility class.
What insoluble means, with an example. The complementary LO-55 class.
Why water's dissolving power matters for the body and nutrient transport. A property tied to its consequence, LO-57.
Whether all liquids mix with water -- vinegar does, oil separates. Sorting liquids by miscibility, LO-55's solubility class extended to liquids.
Heavier means more mass, lighter means less. Naming the physical quantity, LO-59.
Volume as the space matter occupies. Naming the physical quantity, LO-59.
Gram and kilogram for mass. A quantity expressed in SI units, LO-59.
Litre and millilitre for liquid volume. Units for a physical quantity, LO-59.
The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre. LO-59 verbatim.
How materials relate to matter -- materials are the kinds of matter used to make objects. Identification of what a material is, LO-53. The stem has lost a verb ('How does the materials...').
Ayurveda's twenty guna for describing matter. A classification framework, LO-55.
Why classification is useful, shown through a kitchen or grocer's arrangement. LO-55 for the principle and LO-62 because the example is an everyday organising practice.
Lustre explained, and whether a non-metal can look lustrous once polished or coated. Identification by appearance and its limits, LO-53.
Describe the DIFFERENCES between transparent, translucent and opaque with an example each. An explicit three-way differentiation, LO-54, where the single definitions were LO-55.
Define solubility, then describe an activity that shows some substances dissolve and others do not. The activity design is the bulk of the item, LO-56.
What matter is, its two properties and the units used for each. Physical quantities with their units, LO-59.
Ayurveda's classification of matter with examples of its opposing pairs -- guru/laghu, hima/ushna, shlakshana/khara, mridu/kathina. A classification system, LO-55.
Why properties must drive material choice, worked through a pen's parts. LO-62 at essay length.
Harappan pottery techniques and the uses of the pots. A history-of-technology essay; no LO covers ancient craft, so the goal about making things from available materials.
Why sports balls use different materials, related to bounce, weight and durability. Material chosen for a purpose, LO-62.
Conventions for writing kg, L, mL and cubic metre. The form of expressing a quantity in SI units, LO-59.
The carpenter's table: parts (i) and (iii) judge materials against the job (LO-62), part (ii) asks why lustrous screws go dull, which is the air-and-moisture cause (LO-57).
Glass bowl, paper bowl and metal pot judged against what each vessel must do. Selecting materials for a use, LO-62; the transparency naming in part (i) is subordinate to that judgement.
Sand, salt and sugar in water sorted as soluble or insoluble (LO-55), then part (iii) asks why a cloth filter cannot recover dissolved salt (LO-58, explaining the process).
Lemonade ingredients sorted as soluble (LO-55) and part (iii) asks where the droplets on the cold glass come from -- condensation of water vapour, a process to explain (LO-58).
